slides.heading: Transpose Matrix
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Transpose Matrix, an easy arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Flip a 2D matrix over its main diagonal.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Flip a 2D matrix over its main diagonal.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Transposing swaps rows and columns, so the cell at row i, column j moves to row j, column i.
slides.narration: Transposing swaps rows and columns, so the cell at row i, column j moves to row j, column i.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Only one sensible approach: copy every cell once
Must allocate a new C×R matrix (shape changes)
In-place only works for square matrices
slides.narration: There's no faster approach than touching every cell once, so the question is really about getting indices right. Because the shape changes from R by C to C by R, we need a new matrix; an in-place swap only works when the matrix is square.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Allocate a matrix with the dimensions swapped
2. Copy each cell to its mirrored position
slides.narration: Step by step. First, allocate a matrix with the dimensions swapped. Second, copy each cell to its mirrored position. Third, return the new matrix.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: m[0][0] = 1 → t[0][0]
slides.narration: The value 1 at row 0, column 0 moves to row 0, column 0 of the result.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: m[0][2] = 3 → t[2][0]
slides.narration: The value 3 at row 0, column 2 moves to row 2, column 0 of the result.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: m[1][1] = 5 → t[1][1]
slides.narration: The value 5 at row 1, column 1 moves to row 1, column 1 of the result.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: m[1][2] = 6 → t[2][1]
slides.narration: The value 6 at row 1, column 2 moves to row 2, column 1 of the result.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We allocate a matrix with columns and rows swapped, then two nested loops copy matrix i j into result j i.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of w times h. Space is O of w times h.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Don't mix up rows and columns in the loop
slides.narration: The classic bug is allocating the result with the original dimensions. Test a single row and a single column input to catch it.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Follow-up: in-place transpose of a square matrix (swap i<j)
slides.narration: Good follow-ups are an in-place transpose for square matrices, swapping only cells above the diagonal, and rotating an image by ninety degrees, which is a transpose plus reversing each row.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: Transposing swaps rows and columns, so the cell at row i, column j moves to row j, column i.
slides.narration: To recap Transpose Matrix: Transposing swaps rows and columns, so the cell at row i, column j moves to row j, column i. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
